record.paper_title: Space and Time Complexity of Exact Algorithms: Some Open Problems
record.original_question: For SUBSET-SUM, where the input is n positive integers b_1, ..., b_n and a goal sum B and the task is to decide whether some subset of the integers sums to B, construct an exact algorithm running in O*(1.4^n) time, where O* suppresses polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: Construct an O*(1.4n) time algorithm for SUBSET-SUM.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Given $n$ positive integers $b_1,\dots,b_n$ and a target integer $B$, the SUBSET-SUM problem asks whether there exists a subset $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $\sum_{i\in S} b_i = B$. Using the notation $O^*(\cdot)$ to suppress factors polynomial in the input size, construct an exact algorithm solving SUBSET-SUM in time $O^*(1.4^n)$, thereby improving on the classical meet-in-the-middle bound $O^*(2^{n/2}) = O^*(1.4143^n)$.
artifact.status_search_result: Howgrave-Graham and Joux (EUROCRYPT 2010) gave a heuristic algorithm for random SUBSET-SUM instances running in time Õ(2^{0.337n}) ≈ O*(1.263^n), well below 1.4^n; this was later improved by Becker–Coron–Joux to Õ(2^{0.291n}). These results are heuristic for random instances. Deterministic worst-case improvements only achieve 2^{n/2}/poly(n) (Nederlof–Węgrzycki, 2023), still about 1.414^n. Thus the goal of an O*(1.4^n) algorithm is met heuristically but remains open in the deterministic worst-case sense.

status_evidence.title: Improved Classical and Quantum Algorithms for Subset-Sum
status_evidence.snippet: Howgrave-Graham and Joux proposed a heuristic algorithm solving random subset-sum instances in time Õ(2^{0.337n}), breaking the 2^{n/2} bound. Becker–Coron–Joux improved this to Õ(2^{0.291n}).
status_evidence.claim: Heuristic algorithms achieving runtime better than O*(1.4^n) are known.

status_evidence.title: Subset Sum in Time 2^{n/2}/poly(n)
status_evidence.snippet: A deterministic algorithm solving SUBSET-SUM in time 2^{n/2}/poly(n).
status_evidence.claim: Deterministic worst-case algorithms still essentially match the 2^{n/2} ≈ 1.414^n bound.
